transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
- Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Dan Ronan.
Tech giant Nvidia announces its quarterly earnings
this week amid a growing scandal
involving its former CEO, Jensen Wong.
Wong reportedly had a relationship
with a Chinese executive
with a Singapore-based tech company, Megasmede.
Allegedly, she worked for the Chinese Ministry
of State Security.
Rick Mulvey is a reporter with NPR's daily economic show,
The Planet Indicator from Planet Money.
- Investigators at the Commerce Department
raised some flags about this company a couple of years ago.
They thought it was unusual
that Megasmede had Nvidia chips just packed in boxes
at its data center in Malaysia,
sort of like leaving Amazon packages in your entrance way,
except with highly coveted AI chips.
In a statement provided to NPR, Megasmede says
it conducts lawful and legitimate business,
and that Alice Wong left the company last year.
Now, Culper Research, a short seller,
or someone who bets against companies,
noted their uncomfortably close relationship back in May.
So, in other words, there was some smoke
long before this fire.
- Russian attacks killed four people
and injured dozens of others across Ukraine over the weekend.
NPR's Eleanor Beardsley reports.
- Air raid sirens went off throughout Sunday in Kiev
and other cities across the country.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyi said
Russia had launched more than 2,300 attack drones,
1,590 glide bombs, and 15 missiles of various types
against Ukraine over the past week.
He said continued restrictions on the speed of Star Shield,
the militarized version of Starlink,
are preventing Ukrainian interceptor drones
from taking down jet-powered Shahid drones.
Russian forces are targeting energy substations
with the Shahid drones.
Zelenskyi said many of the strikes get through
precisely because speed restrictions remain in place.
Eleanor Beardsley, NPR News, Kiev.
- A federal investigation says leadership failures
at the Grand Canyon National Park allowed a wildfire
to grow out of control last year.
Member Station reporter from KNAU, Adam Scabland,
has more on the story.
- The U.S. Interior Department's report
identifies systemic mismanagement
of last year's Dragon Bravo fire
that destroyed an iconic lodge
on the Grand Canyon's North Rim.
The investigation found poor communication
between the park's superintendent and fire managers
delayed the use of chemical retardant for days
as the fire rapidly spread.
According to the report, park leaders were disconnected
from conditions on the ground
and supported a less aggressive strategy
even as the blaze began to threaten the lives of park staff.
The report proposed nearly 100 firefighting policy changes
in national parks.
Grand Canyon officials didn't immediately respond
to a request for comment.
For NPR News, I'm Adrian Scabland in Flagstaff.
- It's NPR.
California's Pacific Coast is getting pounded
by high waves over the weekend.
More than 50 feet waves were reported
south of San Francisco.
A Super El Nino has warmed the ocean,
leading to an increased volume of seawater in other areas
that was flooding at some ocean-side streets.
Thanksgiving is almost here,
but an earlier than usual flu season means
holiday gatherings could spread illness.
NPR's Sydney Lupkin reports.
- Multiple states are already reporting
high levels of flu-like illnesses.
That's according to the latest flu surveillance data
from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Meanwhile, AAA estimates that 82 million people
are expected to travel more than 50 miles for Thanksgiving.
Small spaces like cars, trains, and planes,
or holiday parties make it easier for the flu to spread.
Here's Claire Hannon, the executive director
of the Association of Immunization Managers.
- The best protection you can get is from the vaccine.
So now is the time to go get it
and to keep yourself safe from serious implications
from influenza.
- She says there should be plenty of vaccines
to protect against flu, COVID, and RSV available
at your local pharmacy or doctor's office.
Sydney Lupkin, NPR News.
- Former Democratic Congresswoman Mary Peltola
is inching closer to the 50% threshold.
She needs to reach the Alaska U.S. Senate race
against incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan.
If she gets to 50%,
it would preclude Alaskan election officials
from using the state's ranked choice voting system.
She currently has 49%.
I'm Dan Roman, NPR News.
- Support for NPR.
- This message comes from IXL.
IXL's Level Up Diagnostic gives immediate benchmark results
along with personalized action plans
that link directly to IXL's skill practice.
More at IXL.com/NPR.

topics.text: Nvidia faces growing scandal over former CEO Jensen Wong's alleged ties to Chinese executive
Russian attacks across Ukraine kill four and injure dozens over the weekend, Zelenskyi says
Interior Department report blames leadership failures for Grand Canyon's Dragon Bravo wildfire
Huge waves pound California's Pacific Coast, with 50-foot waves reported south of San Francisco
Early flu season raises concerns ahead of Thanksgiving holiday travel and gatherings
Mary Peltola nears 50% threshold in Alaska Senate race against Dan Sullivan
